questions.knowledge_point: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation
questions.problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3x}{5xy+y}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3x}{(5x+1)y} \\  & =\frac{3x}{5x+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
y\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3x}{5x+1}
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={3}^{x}\cdot {3}^{-2y}
$$

$$
{3}^{2y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={3}^{x}\,.

questions.problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x+y}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{y}
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{e}^{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x},
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
{e}^{-y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y{e}^{x}$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y{e}^{x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={e}^{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|={e}^{x}+C
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡y}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡y} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡y & ={x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡y={x}^{3}+C.
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$

To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y}$ for $x\ne 0$ and $-\frac{\pi }{2}<y<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y} \\ \operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{sec}⁡y\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{sec}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡y=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x{e}^{-y}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{{e}^{y}} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{e}^{y}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C).
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}+1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={y}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(y) & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(y)=x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+C).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=6x\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6x\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\cdot 3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\int {y}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{1/3} & ={x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{1/3}={x}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=({x}^{2}+C)^{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}={x}^{2}y$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}y \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\frac{1}{3}\,{x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\frac{1}{3}\,{x}^{3}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{3}/3}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{{x}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{{x}^{3}/3}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)y=0$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)y \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}-\sqrt{y}=2x\sqrt{y}$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}-\sqrt{y} & =2x\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\sqrt{y} & =2x\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(2x+1)\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(2x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ 2\sqrt{y} & ={x}^{2}+x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
2\sqrt{y}={x}^{2}+x+C
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}+x+C}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\sqrt{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2}=2{x}^{1/2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C \\ {y}^{3/2} & =3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2})}^{2/3} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+K)}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\frac{3C}{2}.$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $(xy)^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1$ for $x\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}(xy)^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}{y}^{3} & =-\frac{1}{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}=C-\frac{1}{x}.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3} & =C-\frac{1}{x} \\ {y}^{3} & =3C-\frac{3}{x} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{3C-\frac{3}{x}} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{K-\frac{3}{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=3C.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{2}+2{y}^{2}x$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}+2{y}^{2}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}(1+2x) \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int (1+2x)\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =x+{x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
-\frac{1}{y}={x}^{2}+x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+x+C}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $x,y \geq 0,$ separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2xy}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  \sqrt{2x} \cdot  \sqrt{y}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{y} \\ y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+2K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C= 2K.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
y^2 = x^2 + C .
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form
canonical_examples.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' = \dfrac {x^2}{y}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}y^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + C.
$$

We can express the solution in the form $y = y(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = 2C.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating
canonical_examples.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' + 2xy = 0$ for $y\neq 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2xy \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln \vert y \vert = -x^2 + C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y = y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = e^C$  and $K > 0.$ 

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y = Ke^{-x^2}.
$$
